title: Integral birational morphisms to a normal integral scheme are isomorphisms
statement: Let $Z$ and $T$ be integral schemes [def-pc-integral-scheme], with generic points $\eta_Z$ and $\eta_T$ [def-sc-generic-point]. Let $p:Z\to T$ be an integral morphism [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], meaning that for each affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq T$ its inverse image is affine, $p^{-1}U=\operatorname{Spec}B$, and $A\to B$ is integral. Assume $p(\eta_Z)=\eta_T$ and the induced homomorphism of function fields $k(T)=\mathcal O_{T,\eta_T}\to\mathcal O_{Z,\eta_Z}=k(Z)$ [def-sc-function-field] is an isomorphism. Suppose every local ring of $T$ is an integrally closed domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. Then $p$ is an isomorphism of schemes. The morphism $p$ is not assumed finite, and no Noetherian or finite-presentation hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Tag 0AB1, label lemma-finite-birational-over-normal, integral (not necessarily finite) variant and its complete affine proof.

proof.text: Let $U\subseteq T$ be a nonempty affine open and put $V=p^{-1}(U)$, $A=\mathcal O_T(U)$ and $B=\mathcal O_Z(V)$. By the definition of an integral morphism [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], $V$ is affine and $u:A\to B$ is integral. By [lem-sc-integral-function-field-affine-fraction], $\eta_T\in U$; hence $\eta_Z\in V$ by $p(\eta_Z)=\eta_T$, so $V$ is nonempty. Apply that same node to $(T,U)$ and $(Z,V)$: $A,B$ are domains and the germ maps $\alpha:A\hookrightarrow k(T)$ and $\beta:B\hookrightarrow k(Z)$ identify these fields as their respective fraction fields. Write $\phi:k(T)\xrightarrow{\sim}k(Z)$ for the given stalk homomorphism. Naturality of the germ maps gives $\beta u=\phi\alpha$: both send a section on $U$ to its pulled-back germ at $\eta_Z$. Thus $u$ is injective. Via $\alpha$ and $\phi^{-1}\beta$ regard $A\subseteq B\subseteq K=k(T)$; this inclusion of $A$ in $B$ is precisely $u$, and $K$ is a fraction field of $A$.

For any maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $A$, let $t\in U$ be its corresponding point. By [lem-weil-pbc-affine-open-stalk-localization](c), $A_{\mathfrak m}\cong\mathcal O_{T,t}$ through the germ map. The latter ring is an integrally closed domain by hypothesis. The meaning of integral closedness [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring] is invariant under a ring isomorphism: apply the isomorphism to the coefficients and the root of each monic equation. Consequently every $A_{\mathfrak m}$ is a normal domain. Since $A$ is a domain, [lem-weil-pbc-normal-domain-of-local-normal] applies and shows that $A$ is integrally closed in $K$.

source.place: Tag 030B, label lemma-normality-is-local, (3) implies (1), as used by Morphisms Tag 0AB1; affine stalk identification: Schemes Tag 01HV, label lemma-spec-sheaves, (6).

proof.text: For $b\in B$, integrality of $u$ means that $b$ satisfies a monic polynomial $b^d+\sum_{i<d}u(a_i)b^i=0$ with $a_i\in A$ [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism]. Under $B\hookrightarrow K$, the same equation has coefficients $a_i$. Integral closedness of $A$ [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring] therefore puts the image of $b$ in $A$. Choose $a\in A$ with that image. Injectivity of $B\hookrightarrow K$ gives $b=u(a)$. Thus $u$ is surjective as well as injective, so its inverse is a ring homomorphism (apply injectivity to the addition and multiplication identities). The induced map on global sections of $p_U:V\to U$ is $u$. Both schemes are affine, so [lem-sc-affine-global-sections-iso] makes $p_U$ an isomorphism.

Cover $T$ by its nonempty affine opens $U_i$, and let $s_i:U_i\to p^{-1}(U_i)$ be the inverses supplied by Step 3, viewed also as maps to $Z$. On $W=U_i\cap U_j$, each $s_i|_W$ and $s_j|_W$ lands in $p^{-1}(W)$ because its composite with $p$ is the inclusion of $W$. The restriction of $p_{U_i}$ to $p^{-1}(W)$ is an isomorphism to $W$ (restrict its inverse); both maps are its inverses, so they agree by uniqueness of an inverse. By [lem-weil-pbc-scheme-morphism-gluing], the $s_i$ glue to $s:T\to Z$. On every $U_i$, $p s$ is the identity, so the uniqueness clause of that node gives $p s=\mathrm{id}_T$. The opens $p^{-1}(U_i)$ cover $Z$, and $s p$ restricts to $s_i p_{U_i}=\mathrm{id}$ on each; the same uniqueness clause gives $s p=\mathrm{id}_Z$. Therefore $s$ is the inverse of $p$. No intersection $U_i\cap U_j$ is asserted affine, and no finite subcover is used.

source.place: Tag 0AB1, final sentence, with the inverse-gluing argument written out; Schemes Tag 01JJ (label lemma-glue-functors), proof gluing the local morphisms, and Sheaves Tag 00AN (label lemma-mapping-property-glue).
